card.intuition: A network of edge servers spread across the globe that cache static (and some dynamic) content as close to end users as possible, so requests never have to round-trip all the way to the origin datacenter. The origin server is authoritative; edges store copies and refresh them on a schedule or on invalidation.
card.analogy: A chain of local coffee stands stocking the same packaged pastries: instead of every customer traveling to the central bakery (origin), they grab a pastry from the kiosk down the street. When a pastry expires or a new recipe ships, the bakery sends fresh stock out to every kiosk.
card.time_complexity: Cache hit: O(1) retrieval of the asset from the edge node nearest the user; cache miss: one round-trip to the origin plus one edge write.
card.space_complexity: Storage scales with the number of edge points-of-presence times the cached asset set; hot content is replicated near every region.
when_to_use: Serving static assets (images, video, JS, CSS) to a globally distributed audience
Reducing origin load and bandwidth costs for read-heavy, cacheable content
Improving latency and reliability for users far from the origin datacenter
gotchas: Stale content: cached copies can outlive the source unless TTLs, versioned URLs, or purge mechanisms are used
Not a magic bullet: dynamically personalized or rapid-invalidation content requires push/purge APIs and careful cache-key design

steps.annotation: A user requests an asset (e.g. a video or an image) from the nearest edge node.
The edge returns the cached copy on a cache hit, keeping latency low and origin untouched.
On a cache miss, the edge fetches the canonical copy from the origin and caches it locally.
Origin-triggered backends (app + DB) generate or invalidate assets, pushed back out to edges.
Future requests in that region now hit the warmed edge cache until the TTL expires.

exercise.prompt: Compute the TTL needed to hold recently invalidated content: an image is cached at an edge for 12 hours, but the origin pushes a purge after 4 hours. How many hours of stale content were served in the worst case?
exercise.starter_code:
cache_ttl_hours = 12
purge_hours = 4

stale_hours = cache_ttl_hours - purge_hours
# Result is ______ hours
hints: The asset can be served stale until the TTL would have expired naturally
Subtract the time the purge happened from the full TTL
